subtopics.title: Important Formulas
subtopics.subtitle: One-page revision of the chapter's key formulas, topic by topic, plus the numbers to memorise

concepts.text: Every formula below is taught in one of the Chapter 1 subtopics; this page collects the ones that decide most one-mark questions. Read a topic block, cover it, and rewrite the formulas from memory. Symbols follow the subtopics: V_m peak, V_rms effective, φ phase angle, ω = 2πf angular frequency, R_th Thevenin resistance.

concepts.latex: \text{Ohm's law: } V = IR,\qquad P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
concepts.plainText: Ohm's law: V = IR;  P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Resistance: R = ρl/A;  R_t = R_0(1 + αt)
Series: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + …;  Parallel: 1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + …

concepts.latex: \text{Two in parallel: } R_p = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2};\quad n\text{ equal: } R_p = \frac{R}{n}
concepts.plainText: Two in parallel: R_p = R_1R_2/(R_1 + R_2);  n equal resistors: R/n

concepts.latex: \text{Dividers: } V_1 = V\frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2},\qquad I_1 = I\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
concepts.plainText: Voltage divider: V_1 = V·R_1/(R_1 + R_2);  current divider: I_1 = I·R_2/(R_1 + R_2)
Energy: W = P·t;  1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J

concepts.latex: \text{Delta to star: } R_A = \frac{R_{AB} R_{CA}}{R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}},\qquad R_Y = \frac{R_\Delta}{3}
concepts.plainText: Delta→star: R_A = R_AB·R_CA/(R_AB + R_BC + R_CA);  balanced: R_Y = R_Δ/3

concepts.latex: \text{Star to delta: } R_{AB} = R_A + R_B + \frac{R_A R_B}{R_C},\qquad R_\Delta = 3R_Y
concepts.plainText: Star→delta: R_AB = R_A + R_B + R_A·R_B/R_C;  balanced: R_Δ = 3R_Y
KCL: ΣI at a node = 0;  KVL: ΣV around a loop = 0
Thevenin: V_th = V_oc;  R_th = V_oc/I_sc;  I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L)

concepts.latex: \text{Norton: } I_N = I_{sc},\qquad R_N = R_{th},\qquad V_{th} = I_N R_N
concepts.plainText: Norton: I_N = I_sc;  R_N = R_th;  V_th = I_N·R_N
Maximum power: R_L = R_th;  P_max = V_th²/(4R_th);  efficiency 50 %

concepts.latex: \text{Reactance: } X_L = 2\pi f L,\qquad X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
concepts.plainText: X_L = 2πfL;  X_C = 1/(2πfC)
Series RLC: Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²);  tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R
Time constants: τ = L/R (RL), τ = RC (RC); 63.2 % of the final value after one τ
Resonance: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC));  Q = X_L/R = (1/R)√(L/C);  BW = f_r/Q

concepts.latex: \text{Power: } P = VI\cos\phi,\quad Q = VI\sin\phi,\quad S = VI = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2}
concepts.plainText: P = VI cos φ (W);  Q = VI sin φ (VAR);  S = VI = √(P² + Q²) (VA)
Power factor: cos φ = P/S = R/Z
v = V_m sin(ωt + φ);  ω = 2πf = 2π/T

concepts.latex: \text{Generated EMF: } e = NBA\omega\sin\omega t,\qquad E_m = NBA\omega,\qquad f = \frac{PN}{120}
concepts.plainText: e = NBAω sin ωt;  E_m = NBAω;  alternator frequency f = PN/120
Form factor = V_rms/V_avg = 1.11;  peak factor = V_m/V_rms = 1.414

concepts.latex: \text{Star: } V_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_{ph},\; I_L = I_{ph};\qquad \text{Delta: } V_L = V_{ph},\; I_L = \sqrt{3}\,I_{ph}
concepts.plainText: Star: V_L = √3 V_ph, I_L = I_ph;  Delta: V_L = V_ph, I_L = √3 I_ph
P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 3 V_ph I_ph cos φ
Diode: I_D = I_S(e^(V_D/nV_T) − 1);  V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature
I_E = I_B + I_C;  β = I_C/I_B;  α = I_C/I_E
Small-signal: r_e = 26 mV/I_E;  g_m = I_C/V_T;  r_π = β/g_m
MOSFET saturation: I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)²;  g_m = 2k(V_GS − V_T)
CMOS dynamic power: P = C·V_DD²·f
Barkhausen criterion: |Aβ| = 1 and loop phase shift 0° or 360°
RC phase-shift oscillator: f = 1/(2πRC√6);  gain ≥ 29
Wien bridge: f = 1/(2πRC);  gain = 3 (R_f = 2R_1)
Hartley: f = 1/(2π√(L_T C)),  L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M
Colpitts: f = 1/(2π√(L C_T)),  C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2)
555 astable: f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C);  monostable: T = 1.1 RC
Voltage gain (dB) = 20 log(V_o/V_i);  power gain (dB) = 10 log(P_o/P_i)
η = P_ac/P_dc;  class A max 25 % (RC-coupled) / 50 % (transformer);  class B max π/4 = 78.5 %

concepts.latex: \text{Class AB bias: } V_{bias} \approx 2V_{BE};\qquad V_{BE}\text{ multiplier: } V_{bias} = V_{BE}\left(1 + \frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)
concepts.plainText: Class AB bias ≈ 2V_BE;  V_BE multiplier: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R_1/R_2)
Transformer-coupled push-pull: reflected load R_L' = (N_1/N_2)² R_L
Tuned amplifier: f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC));  BW = f_0/Q
Op-amp: inverting gain = −R_f/R_in;  non-inverting gain = 1 + R_f/R_1

rows: RMS / average value of a sine (of V_m)
Form factor / peak factor of a sine
Thermal voltage V_T at room temperature
Max efficiency: class A (RC / transformer) / class B
Oscillator gain needed: RC phase-shift / Wien bridge

concepts.text: A formula is only useful in the exam if you can substitute into it quickly and without unit slips. Each line below is a complete one-step drill: the given values, the formula already filled in, and the result with its unit. Cover the right-hand side, work each line yourself, then check. The lines use round numbers on purpose so that you can also check them by mental arithmetic.

DC circuits and network theorems
R = ρl/A: 100 m of 1.5 mm² copper (ρ = 1.72e-8 Ω·m) -> 1.72e-8 × 100 / 1.5e-6 = 1.15 Ω
P = V²/R: 230 V across 52.9 Ω -> 52 900 / 52.9 = 1000 W
Divider: 12 V across 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ -> V(2 kΩ) = 12 × 2/3 = 8 V
Balanced delta of 30 Ω -> star of 30/3 = 10 Ω per arm
Thevenin: V_oc = 10 V, I_sc = 2 A -> R_th = 5 Ω; P_max = 10²/(4 × 5) = 5 W
RC: 10 kΩ × 47 µF -> τ = 0.47 s; practically settled after 5τ = 2.35 s

AC circuits and three-phase
At 50 Hz: 0.1 H -> X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω;  100 µF -> X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × 1e-4) = 31.8 Ω
Series RLC: R = 6, X_L = 12, X_C = 4 Ω -> Z = √(6² + 8²) = 10 Ω, pf = 6/10 = 0.6 lagging
Resonance: L = 1 mH, C = 1 µF -> f_r = 1/(2π × 3.162e-5) = 5.03 kHz
Sine: V_m = 325 V -> V_rms = 325/√2 = 230 V, V_avg = 0.637 × 325 = 207 V
Alternator: 4 poles at 1500 rpm -> f = 4 × 1500/120 = 50 Hz
Three-phase: 400 V, 20 A, pf 0.8 -> P = 1.732 × 400 × 20 × 0.8 = 11.1 kW

Semiconductor devices
Si diode, 5 V source, 1 kΩ -> I = (5 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 4.3 mA
β = 200 -> α = 200/201 = 0.995
I_C = 2 mA, V_T = 26 mV -> g_m = 2/26 = 76.9 mS; r_e ≈ 26/2 = 13 Ω
MOSFET: k = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V, V_GS = 3 V -> I_D = 1 × 2² = 4 mA; g_m = 2 × 1 × 2 = 4 mA/V
Bridge rectifier, V_m = 20 V, ideal diodes -> V_dc = 0.637 × 20 = 12.7 V

Oscillators and amplifiers
RC phase shift: R = 4.7 kΩ, C = 10 nF -> f = 1/(2π × 4.7e-5 × 2.449) = 1.38 kHz
Wien bridge: R = 22 kΩ, C = 10 nF -> f = 1/(2π × 2.2e-4) = 723 Hz
Colpitts: C_1 = C_2 = 1 nF -> C_T = 0.5 nF; with L = 50 µH -> f = 1.01 MHz
555 astable: R_A = 4.7 kΩ, R_B = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF -> f = 1.44/(24.7k × 10n) = 5.83 kHz
Gain 1000: as a voltage ratio 20 log 1000 = 60 dB; as a power ratio 10 log 1000 = 30 dB
Class B: V_CC = 12 V, R_L = 8 Ω -> P_o(max) = 12²/(2 × 8) = 9 W
Op-amp: R_f = 100 kΩ, R_1 = 10 kΩ -> inverting gain −10, non-inverting gain 11

concepts.plainText: V_avg = (2√2/π)·V_rms = 0.9 V_rms;  overall gain in dB = sum of stage gains in dB

rows: 20 log for voltage or current, 10 log for power
C_T = C_1 C_2 / (C_1 + C_2), the series value
L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M when the coils are coupled
√3 on the current of a star load
Star: I_L = I_ph; delta: I_L = √3 I_ph
r_e = 26 / I_E with I_E in amperes
r_e = 26 mV / I_E; with I_E in mA the result is in ohms
Series resonance gives minimum Z and maximum current

concepts.text: Most wrong answers in formula questions come from prefixes, not formulas. Write every value in base units before substituting (µF = 10⁻⁶ F, nF = 10⁻⁹ F, pF = 10⁻¹² F, mH = 10⁻³ H, kΩ = 10³ Ω) and convert rpm to revolutions per second before using ω = 2πn.

For a quick sanity check, estimate the order of magnitude first: a µH-pF tank lands in the MHz range, an mH-µF tank in the kHz range, and a 10 kΩ, 10 nF RC network near 1.6 kHz. If your worked answer is a factor of 2π, √2, √3 or 1000 away from the estimate, look for the slip before choosing an option.

formulas.latex: V = IR,\qquad P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
formulas.plainText: V = IR;  P = VI = I²R = V²/R
V_rms = 0.707 V_m;  V_avg = 0.637 V_m;  form factor 1.11
Alternator f = PN/120;  three-phase P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ
Phase-shift oscillator f = 1/(2πRC√6);  Wien bridge f = 1/(2πRC)
Class B max efficiency 78.5 %;  voltage gain in dB = 20 log(V_o/V_i)

notes.text: Numeric one-mark questions hide in the constants: 0.707, 0.637, 1.11, 1.414, 0.7 V / 0.3 V, 26 mV, 25 % / 50 % / 78.5 %, 1.44 and 1.1. Learn the table above as a set; the formulas then follow.
Unit slips lose more marks than forgotten formulas: convert mH to H, µF to F and kΩ to Ω before substituting, keep f in Hz, and remember that 1 kWh is 3.6 × 10⁶ J, not 3600 J.

Swap traps to say aloud before answering: series resonance = minimum Z, maximum I; parallel resonance = maximum Z, minimum I. Star: line voltage is √3 × phase voltage; delta: line current is √3 × phase current. Voltage gain uses 20 log, power gain uses 10 log.

formulas.title: Ohm's law and power (all forms)
formulas.latex: V = IR,\qquad P = VI = I^2 R =  rac{V^2}{R}
formulas.plainText: V = IR;  P = VI = I²R = V²/R
formulas.description: V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms, P in watts; any one form of P follows from V = IR.

formulas.title: Maximum power transfer
formulas.description: Load matched to the Thevenin resistance; efficiency is then only 50 %.

formulas.title: Series resonance trio
formulas.latex: f_r =  rac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}},\qquad Q =  rac{X_L}{R},\qquad BW =  rac{f_r}{Q}
formulas.description: L in henries, C in farads; at f_r the impedance equals R and the power factor is 1.

formulas.title: Sine-wave values
formulas.plainText: V_rms = 0.707 V_m;  V_avg = 0.637 V_m (half cycle);  form factor 1.11
formulas.description: V_m is the peak value; the average is taken over a half cycle.

formulas.title: BJT current gains
formulas.description: α = I_C/I_E (just below 1) and β = I_C/I_B (tens to hundreds).

formulas.title: 555 timer and class B efficiency
formulas.plainText: 555 astable f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C);  monostable T = 1.1 RC;  class B max efficiency 78.5 %
formulas.description: R in ohms and C in farads give f in hertz and T in seconds; 78.5 % is π/4.

flashcards.front: Quote the four sine-wave factors: RMS, average, form factor, peak factor.
flashcards.back: V_rms = 0.707 V_m, V_avg = 0.637 V_m (half cycle), form factor 1.11, peak factor 1.414.

flashcards.front: Write the resonance trio for a series RLC circuit.
flashcards.back: f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)), Q = X_L/R = (1/R)√(L/C), bandwidth BW = f_r/Q; at f_r the impedance is R (minimum) and the power factor is 1.

flashcards.front: Maximum efficiencies of class A (RC-coupled), class A (transformer-coupled) and class B amplifiers?

questions.questionText: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel are connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply. The total current drawn is:
questions.explanation: The parallel pair gives 6 × 6/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω; in series with 3 Ω the total is 6 Ω, so I = 12/6 = 2 A.

questions.questionText: A coil has resistance 10 Ω and inductance 0.1 H. Its impedance on a 50 Hz supply is approximately:
questions.explanation: X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.1 = 31.4 Ω, so Z = √(10² + 31.4²) = √1086 ≈ 33 Ω. Adding R and X_L arithmetically (41.4 Ω) is the classic mistake.

questions.questionText: The peak value of a 400 V (RMS) three-phase line voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_m = √2 × V_rms = 1.414 × 400 ≈ 566 V. 693 V would be √3 × 400, which relates line and phase quantities, not peak and RMS.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with Q = 20 is supplied with 10 V at its resonant frequency. The voltage across the inductor is:
questions.explanation: At series resonance the inductor and capacitor voltages are each Q times the supply voltage: V_L = Q × V = 20 × 10 = 200 V, even though they cancel each other in the loop.

questions.questionText: A load consumes 1 kW at a power factor of 0.5 lagging. The apparent power drawn is:
questions.explanation: S = P/cos φ = 1000/0.5 = 2000 VA = 2 kVA; the reactive power is √(2² − 1²) ≈ 1.73 kVAR.

questions.questionText: A 9 V source has an internal resistance of 1.5 Ω. The maximum power it can deliver to any load resistor is:
questions.explanation: P_max = V²/(4R_th) = 81/(4 × 1.5) = 13.5 W, obtained with R_L = 1.5 Ω. 54 W is V²/R, the power the internal resistance would take on short circuit.

questions.questionText: A 20 Ω and a 30 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and the pair is in series with an 8 Ω resistor across a 40 V supply. The current in the 30 Ω resistor is:
A 100 µF capacitor is charged to 200 V. The energy stored in it is:
questions.explanation: W = ½CV² = 0.5 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 200² = 2 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 J; CV = 0.02 is the charge in coulombs, not the energy.

questions.questionText: An uncharged 22 µF capacitor is charged through a 47 kΩ resistor. The time after which it can be taken as fully charged (five time constants) is approximately:
questions.explanation: τ = RC = 47 × 10³ × 22 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.034 s, and 5τ ≈ 5.17 s, by which time the voltage is 99.3 % of its final value.

questions.questionText: A linear network has an open-circuit voltage of 9 V and a short-circuit current of 3 A at its terminals. The current it drives through a 6 Ω load is:
questions.explanation: R_th = V_oc/I_sc = 9/3 = 3 Ω, so I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L) = 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A. 1.5 A ignores R_th.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has L = 0.2 H and C = 5 µF. Its resonant frequency, and the reactance of the inductor at that frequency, are approximately:
questions.explanation: ω_0 = 1/√(LC) = 1/√(10⁻⁶) = 1000 rad/s, so f_r = 1000/2π ≈ 159 Hz and X_L = ω_0 L = 1000 × 0.2 = 200 Ω (equal to X_C = 1/(ω_0 C)). 1000 is ω_0 in rad/s, not a frequency in hertz.

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit has R = 5 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 0.1 µF and is fed with 2 V at its resonant frequency. Its quality factor and the voltage across the capacitor are approximately:
questions.explanation: Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = (1/5)√(10⁻²/10⁻⁷) = 316.2/5 ≈ 63.2, and V_C = Q × V = 63.2 × 2 ≈ 126 V. 316 is √(L/C) alone, the characteristic resistance.

questions.questionText: A coil draws 2 A at a power factor of 0.6 lagging from a 100 V, 50 Hz supply. Its inductance is approximately:
questions.explanation: Z = 100/2 = 50 Ω, R = Z cos φ = 30 Ω, X_L = √(50² − 30²) = 40 Ω, so L = X_L/(2πf) = 40/314.2 ≈ 127 mH. Dividing Z instead of X_L by ω gives 159 mH.

questions.questionText: A sinusoidal voltage has an RMS value of 100 V. Its average value taken over a half cycle is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_m = √2 × 100 = 141.4 V and V_avg = 0.637 V_m = 90 V; equivalently V_avg = V_rms/1.11 = 0.9 V_rms. 63.7 V wrongly applies 0.637 to the RMS value.

questions.questionText: A 400 V three-phase induction motor delivers 15 kW of mechanical output at an efficiency of 90 % and a power factor of 0.8 lagging. Its line current is approximately:
questions.explanation: Input = 15/0.9 = 16.67 kW, and I_L = P/(√3 V_L cos φ) = 16 667/(1.732 × 400 × 0.8) ≈ 30.1 A. Ignoring the efficiency gives 27.1 A; leaving out √3 gives 52.1 A.

questions.questionText: A coil of inductance 0.5 H and resistance 25 Ω is switched onto a 50 V DC supply. The initial rate of rise of current and the final steady current are:
questions.explanation: At t = 0+ the current is zero, so the whole 50 V appears across L: di/dt = V/L = 50/0.5 = 100 A/s. Finally I = V/R = 50/25 = 2 A (equivalently I/τ = 2/0.02 s = 100 A/s).

questions.questionText: A 5.1 V Zener regulator is fed from 12 V through a 230 Ω series resistor and supplies a 10 mA load. The current in the Zener diode is:
questions.explanation: I_S = (12 − 5.1)/230 = 30 mA, and I_Z = I_S − I_L = 30 − 10 = 20 mA. 52 mA ignores the Zener voltage (12/230).

questions.questionText: The phase voltage of a balanced star-connected supply is v = 325 sin ωt V. Each phase feeds a 23 Ω resistor (star load). The total power consumed is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_ph(rms) = 325/√2 = 229.8 V, so P = 3 V_ph²/R = 3 × 229.8²/23 ≈ 6.89 kW. Using the peak value gives 13.8 kW, and using the line voltage (398 V) across each resistor gives 20.7 kW.

questions.questionText: In an 11 kV (line, RMS) three-phase star system with an earthed neutral, the peak voltage between any line conductor and earth is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_ph = 11/√3 = 6.35 kV RMS, and its peak is √2 × 6.35 ≈ 8.98 kV; this sets the insulation stress to earth. 15.6 kV is the peak of the line-to-line voltage.

questions.questionText: A balanced delta load of 90 Ω per phase and a balanced star load of 30 Ω per phase are each connected, in turn, to a 400 V three-phase supply. The total powers they take are:
questions.explanation: Delta: P = 3 × 400²/90 = 5.33 kW. Star: V_ph = 400/√3 = 231 V, P = 3 × 231²/30 = 5.33 kW. The two loads are equivalent because R_Y = R_Δ/3.

questions.questionText: A voltage-divider-biased silicon BJT has R_1 = 40 kΩ, R_2 = 10 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ and V_CC = 15 V. Taking β as very large and V_BE = 0.7 V, V_CE is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_B = 15 × 10/50 = 3 V, V_E = 2.3 V, I_C ≈ I_E = 2.3 mA; V_CE = 15 − 2.3 mA × (2.2 k + 1 k) ≈ 7.64 V. 9.94 V is the collector voltage to ground, not V_CE.

questions.questionText: Which of the following quantities is NOT dimensionless (that is, it has a unit)?
options: The quality factor Q of a resonant circuit
The power factor of a load
The transconductance g_m of a transistor
The current gain β of a BJT
questions.explanation: g_m = ΔI_C/ΔV_BE is a current divided by a voltage, measured in siemens (A/V). Q, power factor and β are ratios of like quantities and have no unit.

questions.questionText: An n-channel enhancement MOSFET obeys I_D = k(V_GS − V_T)² in saturation, with k = 0.25 mA/V² and V_T = 1.5 V. At V_GS = 3.5 V, its drain current and transconductance are:
questions.explanation: I_D = 0.25 × (3.5 − 1.5)² = 1 mA and g_m = 2k(V_GS − V_T) = 2 × 0.25 × 2 = 1 mA/V. Forgetting the factor 2 in g_m gives 0.5 mA/V.

questions.questionText: The supply voltage of a CMOS chip is reduced from 5 V to 3.3 V while its load capacitance and clock frequency stay the same. Its dynamic power becomes approximately what percentage of the original?
questions.explanation: P = C V_DD² f, so the ratio is (3.3/5)² = 0.436, i.e. 43.6 % (a saving of 56.4 %). 66 % wrongly assumes power proportional to V_DD.

questions.questionText: An RC phase-shift oscillator uses three identical sections with R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Its frequency of oscillation is approximately:
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2πRC√6) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴ × 2.449) ≈ 650 Hz. 1.59 kHz is the Wien-bridge formula 1/(2πRC); multiplying by √6 instead of dividing gives 3.90 kHz.

questions.questionText: A balanced three-phase load draws 10 A per line from a 400 V supply at a power factor of 0.9 for 8 hours. The energy it consumes is approximately:
questions.explanation: P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ = 1.732 × 400 × 10 × 0.9 = 6.24 kW, so W = P t = 6.24 × 8 ≈ 49.9 kWh. Leaving out √3 gives 28.8 kWh; ignoring the power factor gives 55.4 kWh.

questions.questionText: Which pair of quantities is measured in the same SI unit?
questions.explanation: Reactance, resistance and impedance are all measured in ohms. Energy (J) and power (W), conductance (S) and resistance (Ω), charge (C) and current (A) differ.

questions.questionText: A Colpitts oscillator has C_1 = C_2 = 200 pF and L = 25 µH. Its frequency of oscillation is approximately:
questions.explanation: C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2) = 100 pF, so f = 1/(2π√(25 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 10⁻¹²)) ≈ 3.18 MHz. Adding the capacitors (400 pF) gives 1.59 MHz.

questions.questionText: A Hartley oscillator has L_1 = 2 mH and L_2 = 1 mH with a mutual inductance of 0.5 mH (aiding), and C = 250 pF. Its frequency of oscillation is approximately:
questions.explanation: L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M = 4 mH, so f = 1/(2π√(4 × 10⁻³ × 250 × 10⁻¹²)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 159 kHz. Ignoring M (3 mH) gives 184 kHz.

questions.questionText: A 555 astable with R_A = R_B = 10 kΩ is to produce a 50 Hz square-ish wave, the same frequency as the mains. The timing capacitor required is approximately:
questions.explanation: f = 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C), so C = 1.44/(30 × 10³ × 50) = 0.96 µF. Using R_A + R_B instead of R_A + 2R_B gives 1.44 µF; leaving out the 1.44 gives 0.67 µF.

questions.questionText: A network passes only half of its input voltage to an equal load resistance (voltage ratio 0.5). Expressed in decibels its gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: Gain = 20 log₁₀ 0.5 = 20 × (−0.301) ≈ −6 dB; the power ratio is 0.25. −3 dB corresponds to half power, i.e. a voltage ratio of 0.707.

questions.questionText: An 8-pole alternator driven at 900 rpm supplies a pure 50 mH inductor. The reactance of the inductor at the generated frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: f = PN/120 = 8 × 900/120 = 60 Hz, so X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 60 × 0.05 ≈ 18.8 Ω. Assuming 50 Hz gives 15.7 Ω; using PN/60 doubles f and gives 37.7 Ω.

questions.questionText: A class A amplifier with a resistive (RC-coupled) collector load draws 10 W from its DC supply. The largest AC output power it can deliver is:
questions.explanation: The maximum efficiency of a series-fed class A stage is 25 %, so P_ac(max) = 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 W. 5 W (50 %) needs transformer coupling, and 7.85 W (78.5 %) is the class B limit.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B push-pull stage runs from ±18 V supplies (V_CC = 18 V) into a 16 Ω load. Its maximum output power and the maximum dissipation in each transistor are approximately:
questions.explanation: P_o(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L) = 324/32 ≈ 10.1 W. Each transistor's worst-case dissipation is V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 324/(9.87 × 16) ≈ 2.05 W, about one fifth of P_o(max); 4.10 W is the total for both.

questions.questionText: An inverting summing amplifier has R_f = 10 kΩ and two input resistors of 5 kΩ each. With inputs of 0.5 V and 1 V, the output voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_o = −R_f(V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2) = −10k × (0.5/5k + 1/5k) = −(1 + 2) = −3 V. The inverting configuration makes the sign negative.

questions.questionText: Two identical heating elements are connected first in series and then in parallel across the same supply. The ratio of the power taken in parallel to the power taken in series is:
questions.explanation: With each element R, series gives 2R and parallel gives R/2. With V fixed, P = V²/R_eq, so P_par/P_ser = (2R)/(R/2) = 4.

questions.questionText: An op-amp connected as a voltage follower (output tied directly to the inverting input, signal on the non-inverting input) has a voltage gain of:
questions.explanation: With R_f = 0 and R_1 open, the non-inverting gain 1 + R_f/R_1 = 1; the follower buffers a source with very high input and very low output impedance.

questions.questionText: Taking the electron charge as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the number of electrons that make up a charge of one coulomb is about:
questions.explanation: n = Q/e = 1/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons, so a current of 1 A is a flow of 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.

questions.questionText: Which of the following oscillator formulas is NOT correct?
options: Hartley: total inductance L_T = L_1 + L_2 + 2M
Colpitts: total capacitance C_T = C_1 + C_2
questions.explanation: In a Colpitts oscillator the two tank capacitors are in series around the loop, so C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2); the other three expressions are standard.

questions.questionText: Which statement drawn from different parts of Chapter 1 is NOT correct?
options: In a star connection, line current equals phase current
The form factor of a sine wave is 1.11
The maximum efficiency of a class B push-pull stage is 78.5 %
At series resonance the circuit current is minimum
questions.explanation: At series resonance the impedance is minimum (equal to R), so the current is maximum; it is the parallel (rejector) circuit whose line current is minimum at resonance.

questions.questionText: The approximate forward (knee) voltage of a germanium diode is:
questions.explanation: Germanium diodes begin to conduct appreciably at about 0.2 V to 0.3 V, against about 0.7 V for silicon; 1.1 eV is the band gap of silicon, not a knee voltage.

questions.questionText: A 20 µF capacitor is connected across a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The current it draws is approximately:
A series circuit with R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω and X_C = 40 Ω is connected to a 100 V AC supply. The active power it consumes is:
questions.explanation: Z = √(30² + (80 − 40)²) = 50 Ω, I = 100/50 = 2 A, P = I²R = 4 × 30 = 120 W (pf 0.6). 200 W is the apparent power VI and 160 W is the reactive power in VAR.

questions.questionText: A coil of 200 turns, each of area 0.01 m², rotates at 1500 rpm in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The RMS value of the generated EMF is approximately:
A current i = 14.14 sin 314t A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_rms = 14.14/√2 = 10 A, so P = I_rms²R = 100 × 10 = 1000 W. Using the peak current gives 2000 W, which is the peak instantaneous power.

questions.questionText: When a pn junction is reverse biased, its depletion region:
options: Widens and the junction capacitance falls
Narrows and the junction capacitance rises
questions.explanation: Reverse bias pulls majority carriers away from the junction, widening the depletion layer; the wider 'dielectric' lowers the transition capacitance, which is how varactor diodes work.

questions.questionText: A single-phase 10 kVA transformer has a 230 V secondary. Its full-load secondary current is approximately:
questions.explanation: I = S/V = 10 000/230 ≈ 43.5 A. 25.1 A wrongly uses the three-phase formula S/(√3 V).

questions.questionText: An inverting amplifier with a gain of −10 is followed by a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11. The overall voltage gain and its magnitude in decibels are approximately:
questions.explanation: Cascaded gains multiply: (−10) × 11 = −110, and 20 log₁₀ 110 ≈ 40.8 dB (20 dB + 20.8 dB). Adding the gains instead (21) is the classic mistake.

questions.questionText: A lamp rated 100 W on a 230 V DC supply is connected to a sinusoidal supply whose PEAK value is 230 V. Assuming its resistance stays constant, the power it takes is:
questions.explanation: R = 230²/100 = 529 Ω. The RMS value is 230/√2 = 162.6 V, so P = 162.6²/529 = 50 W: halving V² halves the power. 70.7 W wrongly scales P by 1/√2.

questions.questionText: The product of a resistance in ohms and a capacitance in farads, RC, has the unit of:
questions.explanation: Ω × F = (V/A) × (C/V) = C/A = s, which is why RC is called the time constant; L/R likewise comes out in seconds.
